claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its derivatives are governed by a magnetically tuned phase-transformation mechanism.
Removing or reducing Mn lowers magnetic frustration.
Reduced magnetic frustration lowers the energetic barrier for an FCC-to-HCP transformation.
Dislocation slip and interactions with internal boundaries can trigger an FCC-to-HCP transformation in CrCoNi.
The deformation-induced HCP phase forms at lattice defects or interface regions.
The transformation produces a fine-scale mixture of FCC and HCP domains.
FCC-HCP phase transformation strengthens CrCoNi without compromising plastic deformation.
Mn-containing or Mn-rich derivatives suppress the FCC-to-HCP transformation because Mn introduces magnetic frustration.
Suppression of the transformation causes different dislocation and slip behavior in Mn-containing alloys.
The equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi baseline exhibits minimal or no deformation-induced HCP transformation because of Mn-related magnetic frustration.
All Mn-depleted or Mn-free subsets, or compositions emphasizing Co and Cr, should develop deformation-induced HCP phase.
Mn-depleted alloys should have higher yield strength than equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi because of the transformation.
Mn depletion should alter strain-hardening behavior relative to equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi.
HCP formation should be detectable through diffraction signatures and local microstructural changes.
The investigation will compare the quinary baseline with Mn-depleted and Mn-free alloys processed under identical conditions.
Room-temperature tensile testing with concurrent diffraction and electron microscopy will measure transformation and mechanical behavior.
The hypothesis is limited to initially single-phase FCC Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-family alloys with metastable solid solutions.
The mechanism may not apply to refractory BCC alloys or alloys produced using fundamentally different processing histories.
